notes.meaning: God took the first step by sending the prophet Nathan to David, about nine months after David sinned. Nathan did not attack the king right away, but wisely told a story about two men in a city, one rich and the other poor. God does not leave His people alone in their sin, but lovingly seeks them out to bring them to repentance.

Nathan explained that the rich man owned great numbers of sheep and cattle, while the poor man had only one little ewe lamb that he raised as a family pet. The poor man loved the lamb like a daughter, sharing his food and drink with it and holding it close. This picture highlighted the contrast between David, who had many wives, and Uriah, who had only Bathsheba.

When a traveler arrived for a visit, the rich man refused to take an animal from his own large flock. Instead, he stole the poor neighbor's beloved lamb and cooked it for his guest. This showed the extreme selfishness of taking what belongs to someone else to satisfy an appetite.

David was furious at the rich man and swore by the Lord that such a cruel person deserved to die. He also ordered that the thief must repay four sheep for the one he stole, which was the exact penalty in God's law for sheep-stealing. David easily recognized and condemned greed in someone else, even while his own conscience remained blind to his far greater crime.

Nathan boldly broke the truth to the king by saying, "You are that man!" Speaking for God, he reminded David that the Lord made him king, saved him from King Saul, and gave him the royal house and kingdom. God had treated David with great generosity and was willing to give him even more if he had asked.

Nathan asked why David showed contempt for God's word by doing such evil right in front of Him. Even though Uriah died in battle by Ammonite soldiers, God held David fully guilty of murdering him. Sin cannot be hidden behind human plots, because God sees who is truly to blame.

Because David turned his back on God and took Uriah's wife, the Lord declared that violence and death would never leave David's own family during his reign. Despising God's commands is the same as despising God Himself. David's household would soon be torn apart by bitter conflict among his own children.

God told David that trouble would rise up against him from inside his own home. Because David acted in secret when he took another man's wife, a family member would openly take David's wives in broad daylight for the whole nation to see. God permitted this painful public shame to show how seriously He takes secret sin.

David made no excuses and offered no defense, but humbly confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan immediately answered that the Lord took away his sin, so David would not die. God showed deep mercy by pardoning David and sparing him from the death penalty required by the law for murder and adultery.

Nathan explained that because David's public scandal gave God's enemies a reason to mock and dishonor the Lord, the baby boy would die. Even when God forgives the guilt of sin, He sometimes lets painful earthly consequences remain to protect His holy name. God will not let anyone treat His holiness as a light matter.

Nathan went home, and the Lord struck the newborn baby with a very serious illness. The text specifically refers to the mother as Uriah's wife, showing that David's wedding could not erase how the relationship began. God's discipline began immediately to rest on David's house.

David begged God to spare the baby, going without food and lying on the bare ground night after night. The older leaders of his household tried to help him get up and eat, but David refused to listen. He completely humbled himself before God in prayer, hoping the Lord might still show mercy while the child lived.

On the seventh day of the illness, the child passed away. David's servants were terrified to break the news because they worried he would harm himself in his deep sorrow. When David noticed the servants whispering, he figured out what happened, asked them straight out, and they told him the child was dead.

David immediately stood up, washed, put on clean clothes, and went to the house of the Lord to worship. Afterward, he returned home and asked for a meal, and he ate. Instead of growing bitter, David accepted God's final decision with deep submission and worship.

The servants were confused and asked David why he acted this way. He had cried and fasted while the baby was sick, but as soon as the child died, he got up and ate. In their culture, public mourning usually began only after someone died, so David's actions surprised them.

David explained that he fasted while the child was alive because God might graciously decide to heal him. Once death occurred, weeping and fasting could not bring the boy back. David found peace in knowing that while the child could not return to earth, David would one day go to be with him in the presence of God.

David comforted Bathsheba, and in time she gave birth to another son whom they called Solomon, meaning "peaceful." The Lord loved this child and sent Nathan to give him the special name Jedidiah, which means "beloved of the LORD." This was a comforting sign that God had truly restored peace and favor to David and Bathsheba.

During this time, General Joab fought against the Ammonite capital city of Rabbah and seized its water supply. Joab sent messengers urging David to gather the rest of the army and capture the inner fortress himself. Joab wanted his king to have the honor and credit for the final victory.

David assembled the remaining soldiers, marched to Rabbah, and took the city and its great treasures. He took the heavy golden crown from the Ammonite king's head, which was decorated with precious stones, and placed it on his own head. God gave Israel total victory over their fierce enemies.

David brought out the Ammonite prisoners and assigned them to hard labor with saws, iron tools, and brick kilns. He put all the Ammonite towns under this forced labor before returning home to Jerusalem with his troops. Israel's enemies were completely subdued so they could no longer harm God's people.
